channelTitle: The government banned him - so the villages put the masks back on - Part 2
hook: In Part 1, we met Krampus - the horned shadow of St. Nicholas who punished naughty Alpine children. Now, what happened when the authorities tried to kill the tradition off.
storyParts: In the nineteen thirties, Austria's government actually banned Krampus outright, calling the tradition unwholesome and frightening. For a while it worked - the masks went into attics and the runs stopped.

But traditions that old do not die in a closet. After the war the masks came back out, and by the nineteen eighties the Krampuslauf - the Krampus run - had become a full festival: hundreds of men in hand-carved masks and real goat hides charging through snowy streets.
A single proper Krampus mask takes a carver months - the wood, the real horns, the sheepskin. The best ones are passed down through families like heirlooms, and a good suit can cost thousands.

And the postcards - in the early nineteen hundreds, sending Gruss vom Krampus, greetings from Krampus, was a full-blown craze, like a spooky version of valentine mail. Collectors pay real money for them today.

Folks still argue about whether scaring kids is right - but ask an Austrian grandmother and she will tell you Krampus was never really about punishment. He is the shadow that makes the December lights warmer.
cta: Did your family have a scary December figure, or was everyone too nice for that? Tell Grandma June in the comments.
moral: Every winter needs its shadow - Krampus is the growl that makes the kindness of the season glow brighter.
seriesTitle: Krampus Night - Grandma June Story Time
